cells.tense: The lid is off and the cup sits on the table with nothing in it yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and leave it unmeasured today. Water it if it needs water and then walk away. No checking to see if it moved.
cells.core:
Nothing has arrived, and you're already open to it. The cup is out before anyone pours — that's the readiness itself, with no strings attached. You can feel something taking shape without grabbing at it or deciding ahead of time what it should turn into.

That openness doesn't cost you your edges. You're not dissolving into whatever is growing, and you're not holding it off either. That honest middle is what lets a thing come toward you and be met as itself. Keep the cup clean while it fills: whatever you're watching is yours to tend only as long as you're still a person at the table too. The openness is the point, not the waiting for it to be over.
cells.sheetLine: Open to what's growing without forcing it open.
cells.verb: staying open to what hasn't shown itself yet
cells.place: the tending of something still too small to say what it will become

cells.tense: You're hovering over the garden before anything has sprouted, checking it a dozen times a day.
cells.ask: Choose the one thing that most needs you to stop, and leave it alone until tomorrow evening. Say out loud what you're afraid won't happen. Then no checking until then.
cells.core:
You're out ahead of it — reading the soil, planning the bloom, doing next month's work this morning. The attention you're spending is genuine, and it's aimed at a version that isn't here yet. So you miss what's on the table right now, which is nothing more than a start.

Readiness turns into managing when you can't leave something open. You keep trying to close the circle early because open is uncomfortable. Pick one thing you're tending and let it stay unfinished today. Name what you're braced for, then stop. What's growing doesn't need you to hold it to a date, and you don't need it finished to know you're doing this well.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that has already closed behind you, still waiting to be let in.
cells.ask: Tell one person one true sentence about what you hope for. Then stop talking and let it stand on its own.
cells.core:
You had a cup on the table once, and it came back in a way you didn't plan for. Now the cup stays on the shelf. Nothing gets poured because you stopped setting it out, and that choice is a while back, made by you, not revisited since.

Something in you is parked, not gone. Say out loud what you actually want without adding the plan for it or the reasons it might not happen, and you may notice the closed door is behind you rather than ahead. Plain presence is the ground you can come back to. Nothing more is asked of you today than to be here without an agenda.

cells.tense: The cup is already out and open on the table; you keep saying you don't do that.
cells.ask: Name one thing you hold a place for. Write 'this matters to me' beside it, and show no one. Notice the room you kept is on your side of the ledger too.
cells.core:
You're open already. People can tell in how you listen, how long you wait, what you bother to make space for — and you file it under keeping the peace, or just being there, or nothing much. The readiness runs without your name on it.

The open cup does its work anyway. Call yourself open to something and it becomes a fact about you, not just about the room. Leaving it unnamed kept it from feeling like a debt you owed — but it was a gift the whole time, and a gift means you're allowed to receive back. The plain word for what you do is care. Say it about one thing, and it gets an owner.
cells.sheetLine: You're already open. You just won't say it's yours.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person was ever turned away — the record says the feeling is nascent now, not that it was ever refused. A reader could reasonably say they simply trust slowly and always have. The ask survives being wrong because it points at a witness, not at a wound; if nothing was ever refused, telling one person a true thing is still worth doing. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'the lid is off and the cup is set down,' which sounds like a small poem and asks nothing — I've cut the rest of that ornament and kept only the plain fact.
